title: 8,000 Steam Demos: Why Finding a Good One Feels Like a Lottery

scenes.title: Overview — the blurred Next Fest front page
lines: Hello, this is Yamyam Coding.
What you are looking at is the front page of the Steam Next Fest running today. Every blurred tile is a demo whose developer wrote down that generative AI was used.
A Reddit post saying that AI has absolutely ruined Next Fest passed eight thousand upvotes. Is that really what happened?

Today we will look at the situation that post came from, read the rules for how Steam makes developers disclose AI use, compare the numbers people actually counted across three fests, and finally see what players and studios are choosing to do right now.
Let us start with that Reddit post.

scenes.title: Phenomenon — 8,202 demos and a lottery
lines: This Next Fest, which opened on October 19, has more than eight thousand two hundred demos. That is more than double the same event last year.
The very next day, a post on the Steam subreddit said that Next Fest had been absolutely ruined by AI, and by the twentieth it had passed eight thousand eight hundred upvotes.
In the author's words, finding a decent demo is harder than winning the lottery. The most upvoted comment was a single line: they did not want to take part at all.
But the feeling that everything is AI and the actual number can be two different things. People have counted.
Before we look at the numbers, we need to know what those numbers count. That is Steam's disclosure rule.

scenes.title: Principle — the AI Generated Content Disclosure
lines: On January 10, 2024, Valve announced how it would handle games that use AI.
The Content Survey that developers fill out when submitting a game gained an AI section, and it splits AI use into two kinds.
One is Pre-Generated: content made with AI tools during development, such as art, code or sound, that ships inside the game files.

The other is Live-Generated: content the AI creates while the game is running. This one carries an extra condition. The developer has to describe what guardrails, meaning safety measures, keep it from producing illegal content.
Valve uses the survey in its pre-release review and publishes much of it on the store page as written.
Scroll the demo page on screen all the way down and you reach this box. It is called the AI Generated Content Disclosure. Every number in today's video is a count of this box.
Live-Generated games get one more thing: players can report content that slipped past the guardrails straight from the in-game overlay.

One condition matters here. The survey was revised early this year, and the scope became explicit. This section covers only content that ships with the game and that players see and hear. Efficiency gains from development tools are stated to be outside its focus.

So a developer who used an AI coding assistant does not have to disclose it, while one who made the capsule art or background music with AI does. The disclosure count is a count of AI that appears on screen.

scenes.title: Confirmation — numbers from three fests
lines: Now the numbers.

February's fest had three thousand four hundred fifty-six demos, and ten of the top one hundred on the popular-demos chart carried a disclosure. Four of those ten were for placeholder images or music.
June's fest had one thousand seven hundred four disclosures among eight thousand seven hundred demos: 19.5 percent.

And this October's fest has two thousand five hundred ninety-five among the seven thousand one hundred forty-five listed on SteamDB: over 36 percent. In four months it went from one in five to more than one in three.

There are cautions in both directions. Developers write the disclosure themselves, so games that did not write one were not counted; the real figure may be higher. On the other hand, a single placeholder image puts a game in the same box. That 36 percent is not all games made with AI.
The share you feel on the front page can be higher still. In June a reporter clicked sixteen tiles on the hub's front page and ten of them raised a warning.
I clicked sixteen tiles the same way on today's front page. The result is written on screen exactly as measured.

scenes.title: Variation — why 36 percent looks like everything
lines: So why does 36 percent feel like everything? Three things overlap.

First, sorting. For the first few days the Next Fest hub shuffles most of its sections at random. Only after Steam has learned from player reactions, this time from early Thursday morning Korean time, does it switch to personalized recommendations.

So the front page in the first two days is not a popularity ranking; it is closer to a sample that shows the overall ratio as it is. The top of the charts, in fact, is mostly games without a disclosure.
Second, position. The disclosure sits at the very bottom of the page, so you do not see it until you are about to press install.

Third, first impressions. What you see on the hub is capsule art, the small cover image, and one publisher's lead said that AI-made capsules are an immediate turn-off. Games get filtered by the picture before anyone reads the disclosure.

scenes.title: Depth — what players, Valve and studios chose
lines: So people built their own tools. The blurred tiles in the opening shot are exactly that.

It is an open-source extension called AI warning for Steam. When you open a store page it shows the bottom-of-page disclosure as a pop-up right away, and in search results it blurs or hides games that have one. It runs in Firefox and Chrome and the source is public.

Its limits are clear too. It works only in a browser, and it catches only games that wrote a disclosure. Games that did not cannot be filtered. Valve has not yet answered requests for a filter of its own.
Studios are moving as well. One developer planned a public demo for this fest, cancelled it three days before, and replaced it with a closed test for a small number of people chosen by lottery.

They gave two reasons: the worry that once gameplay spreads, AI-made imitations could ship before the real game, and the judgment that they did not have the staff to enforce rules like a streaming ban.
Whether a studio uses AI or not, the way demos are released is itself changing.

scenes.title: Closing — the number, the feeling and the choices
lines: To sum up: more than a third of the demos in this fest disclose generative AI, a big jump from four months ago.

But the feeling that it is ruined is larger than the number, because random sorting, a disclosure hidden at the bottom, and capsule first impressions overlap. The disclosure counts only AI that appears on screen, and a single placeholder image lands in the same box.
What you can do right now is clear: browse by charts and wishlists, set your own filter with the extension, or scroll to the bottom and read that box.
Studios, for their part, are choosing between adding the disclosure, closing their demos, or putting hand-drawn capsules out front.
